transcript.heading: News Report One (British Female)
paras: A supermarket chain in the United Kingdom has announced that it will remove all "best before" dates from fresh fruit and vegetable products in an effort to reduce food waste. The company says that best before dates are often misunderstood by consumers, who throw away perfectly good food simply because the date on the package has passed, even though the food is still safe and edible to eat. Instead of printed dates, the supermarket will encourage customers to use their own judgment—looking, smelling, and tasting food to decide if it's still good to eat. The move is expected to prevent thousands of tons of food from being wasted every year. Environmental groups have praised the decision, noting that food waste is a major contributor to greenhouse gas emissions when it decomposes in landfills. Other supermarket chains are reportedly considering similar changes, and the UK government has said it supports efforts to help consumers reduce waste in their homes.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Male)
paras: Researchers at Stanford University have developed a new type of flexible, wearable battery that can be stretched, bent, and even washed without losing its ability to hold a charge. The battery, which is thinner than a credit card, uses a special type of polymer that stores energy and can stretch up to twice its original size without breaking. Unlike traditional lithium-ion batteries, which contain hard metal components and can be dangerous if damaged, the new battery is completely soft and flexible, making it ideal for use in wearable technology like smart watches, fitness trackers, and even medical devices that are worn directly on the skin. The researchers say the battery can be recharged hundreds of times and maintains about 80 percent of its capacity after being stretched repeatedly. They are currently working with several technology companies to commercialize the product, and hope to see it in consumer devices within the next three years. Potential applications also include smart clothing with built-in sensors and electronics.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (British Male)
paras: The Norwegian government has announced plans to build the world's first ship tunnel, a massive underwater passage that will allow large cargo ships and passenger ferries to sail through a mountain instead of navigating around a dangerous stretch of coastline. The Stad peninsula in western Norway is known for its rough seas, strong currents, and frequent storms, which often cause delays and accidents for ships traveling along the coast. The 1.7-kilometer-long tunnel will be built through solid rock under the mountain, creating a safe, sheltered shortcut that will save ships about 30 minutes of travel time and eliminate the risk of bad weather forcing vessels to wait for conditions to improve. Construction is expected to begin next year and take about four years to complete, with an estimated cost of 300 million dollars. When finished, it will be the first tunnel of its kind in the world designed specifically for large ships, and may serve as a model for similar projects in other countries with dangerous coastlines.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Leo): Hey Nora, I saw you at the coffee shop yesterday—you were working on your laptop for hours. What were you working on?

Woman (Nora): Oh hey Leo. I was working on my application for the study abroad program. I want to go to Japan next semester, and there's so much paperwork to do—essays, recommendation letters, transcript requests... It's kind of overwhelming.
Man: Study abroad in Japan? That sounds amazing! I've always wanted to go there. Is it through the university's exchange program?

Woman: Yeah, it's a direct exchange with Waseda University in Tokyo. I've been studying Japanese for two years now, and I think living there would really help me improve my language skills. Plus, I'm really interested in Japanese literature and film, so it would be great to experience that culture firsthand.
Man: That makes total sense. But why does it feel overwhelming? I thought study abroad applications were straightforward.

Woman: Well, there's the academic application, but then there's also the visa application, housing arrangements, figuring out health insurance, and of course worrying about money. Tuition is covered by the exchange, but living expenses in Tokyo are really expensive. I'm not sure if I'll be able to afford it.

Man: Have you looked into scholarships? I remember there are several study abroad scholarships you can apply for through the international programs office. Some of them cover living expenses and even airfare.

Woman: I've looked at a couple, but most of them have really competitive applications, and I don't think my grades are good enough. I have a 3.4 GPA, but I feel like everyone who applies has like a 3.8 or higher.

Man: Don't sell yourself short! A 3.4 is still really good, and scholarships look at more than just grades—they care about your essays, your extracurricular activities, your motivation. You should definitely apply for as many as you can. The worst they can say is no, right?
Woman: You're probably right. I just don't want to get my hopes up and then be disappointed if I don't get in or can't afford it.

Man: Well, you won't know unless you try. And even if you don't get scholarships, there are other options—student loans, working part-time while you're there, doing a crowdfunding campaign. My cousin did a study abroad in Korea and raised part of the money that way.
Woman: Hmm, I hadn't thought about crowdfunding. That's an interesting idea. I guess I should just focus on putting together the best application I can and worry about the money later.
Man: That's the spirit! If you need help with your essays or anything, let me know. I've done a lot of writing for my classes, and I'd be happy to proofread for you.
Woman: Thanks, Leo! That would actually be really helpful. I'm never sure if my writing sounds good or not.
Man: No problem. Just send me whatever you have when you're ready, and I'll take a look. You're going to get in—just you wait!

Man: It's... okay, I guess. It's not amazing, but it's not terrible either. There's usually a decent variety—they have a salad bar, a sandwich station, hot meals, pizza, pasta, that kind of thing. But the quality can be really inconsistent. Some days the food is actually pretty good, and other days it's just... bland and boring. And the vegetables are always overcooked.
Woman: I know what you mean. What about the hours? Do you find the dining hall is open when you need it?

Man: That's actually my biggest complaint. On weekdays they close at 8 PM, which is really early if you have evening classes or if you're studying late in the library. And on weekends they open late and close early, so if you sleep in you miss breakfast. I wish they were open later, especially on weekends.
Woman: Yeah, I've heard that from a lot of students. Is there anything you do like about the dining hall?

Man: Well, I do like that there are always options for different dietary needs. I'm vegetarian, and there's usually at least one vegetarian option at every meal, plus the salad bar and the soup station. They've gotten a lot better about that in the past year or two. And I like that it's all-you-can-eat, so I never go hungry.

If you eat three meals a day every day, it works out to a reasonable price per meal, but I don't always eat three meals there. Sometimes I skip breakfast, or I eat off campus with friends. So for me, it's probably not the best value. But it is convenient— I don't have to cook or grocery shop, which saves a lot of time.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: The Great Wall of China is one of the most famous and impressive structures in the world, but many common beliefs about it are actually myths. For example, contrary to popular belief, the Great Wall cannot be seen from space with the naked eye—this is a persistent myth that has been debunked by astronauts and satellite imagery. Another misconception is that it's a single, continuous wall; in reality, the Great Wall is a series of walls, fortifications, and natural barriers built by different dynasties over thousands of years.

Construction of defensive walls in northern China began as early as the 7th century BC, during the Warring States period, when individual kingdoms built walls to protect their borders from neighboring states and nomadic tribes. When Qin Shi Huang unified China in 221 BC, he ordered the connection and extension of these existing walls to create a unified defense system against invasions from the north. This was the first version of what would become the Great Wall.

Most of the wall that tourists visit today, however, was built much later, during the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644 AD). The Ming Wall is the most well-preserved and most famous section, stretching over 8,850 kilometers across mountains, deserts, and rivers. It was built using a variety of materials including brick, stone, tamped earth, and wood, with watchtowers placed at regular intervals for soldiers to keep watch and signal warnings with smoke or fire.

While the wall was effective at times at deterring small-scale raids, it ultimately failed to stop major invasions. The Mongols successfully invaded China in the 13th century, and the Manchus broke through the wall in the 17th century to establish the Qing Dynasty. Historians note that walls alone can never fully protect a civilization—they are only as effective as the soldiers defending them and the political will behind them.

Today, the Great Wall is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of China's most popular tourist attractions, drawing millions of visitors every year. While much of the wall has fallen into disrepair or been destroyed over the centuries, efforts are ongoing to preserve and restore the most important sections for future generations.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: Color psychology is the study of how colors affect human behavior, emotions, and decision-making. While some claims about color psychology are exaggerated or unscientific, research has shown that colors can indeed have measurable effects on our moods, perceptions, and even physical reactions.

One of the most well-documented effects is the impact of red on performance and arousal. Studies have found that seeing the color red can increase heart rate and blood pressure, creating a sense of excitement or urgency. This is why red is often used in fast food restaurant logos and sale signs—it grabs attention and creates a sense of urgency that encourages people to act quickly. However, research has also found that exposure to red can actually worsen performance on analytical tasks like exams, because it creates feelings of stress and avoidance. One study found that students who saw a red cover on their test booklet before an exam scored significantly worse than those who saw green or black covers.

Blue, on the other hand, tends to have a calming, relaxing effect. It is associated with trust, stability, and professionalism, which is why many banks and tech companies use blue in their branding. Research has found that blue environments can lower blood pressure and heart rate, and that people are more productive in blue rooms when doing creative work. However, too much blue can feel cold or impersonal, which is why many offices use warm accent colors along with blue to create balance.

Green is associated with nature, growth, and health, and it tends to have a calming, refreshing effect. Studies have found that hospital patients recover faster when their rooms have views of nature and green spaces, and that workers with plants in their offices report lower stress levels and higher productivity. Green is also often used to signal safety and permission, which is why traffic lights use green for "go."

Of course, the effects of color are not universal—they can be influenced by culture, personal experience, and context. For example, while white is associated with purity and weddings in Western cultures, it is the color of mourning in many East Asian cultures. And individual preferences for colors are shaped by personal memories and associations. But despite these variations, the basic psychological effects of certain colors appear to be consistent across different populations, making color psychology a useful tool in design, marketing, and even healthcare.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: Urban farming—the practice of growing food in cities—has been growing in popularity around the world as people look for ways to eat healthier, reduce their environmental impact, and build stronger communities. From small window boxes and rooftop gardens to large community farms and vertical growing operations, urban agriculture takes many forms and offers a surprising number of benefits.

One of the most obvious benefits is access to fresh, nutritious food. In many cities, especially in low-income neighborhoods known as "food deserts," there are no full-service grocery stores selling fresh produce, and residents rely on convenience stores and fast food restaurants that mostly sell processed, unhealthy food. Urban farms and community gardens can bring fresh vegetables and fruits to these neighborhoods, making healthy food more accessible and affordable for residents who need it most.

Environmental benefits are also significant. Food typically travels hundreds or even thousands of miles from farm to table, requiring large amounts of fossil fuels for transportation and refrigeration, and generating significant greenhouse gas emissions. Growing food locally eliminates these transportation emissions, and urban farms can also help reduce the "urban heat island" effect by replacing concrete and asphalt with plants that provide shade and cool the air through transpiration. Rooftop gardens can also insulate buildings, reducing the energy needed for heating and cooling.

Community benefits are perhaps the most surprising and most important. Community gardens bring people together from different backgrounds, creating social connections and building neighborhood cohesion. People who garden together get to know their neighbors, share skills and knowledge, and work together toward a common goal. For children, gardening provides hands-on education about where food comes from, nutrition, and science, and studies have found that kids who grow their own vegetables are more likely to eat them and develop healthy eating habits that last a lifetime.

Urban farming also has economic benefits. It can create jobs in farming, distribution, and food processing, and it can help revitalize neglected neighborhoods by turning vacant, trash-filled lots into productive, beautiful green spaces. Some urban farms sell their produce at farmers markets or to local restaurants, generating income for the community and supporting the local economy.

While urban farming alone can't solve all the problems of food insecurity or environmental degradation, it is a powerful tool that can make cities healthier, more sustainable, and more connected places to live.
